# UDRP Complaint — Outline

## When to use this

Use this when someone has registered a domain name that is identical or
confusingly similar to the Kingdom's mark, and did so in bad faith — to sell it to
the Kingdom, to impersonate the Kingdom, to divert people looking for the Kingdom,
or to hold it hostage. The Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy is a
contractual arbitration that every registrant of a gTLD accepts as a condition of
registration, so it binds the respondent whether or not they will engage with the
Kingdom on anything else. It transfers domains without a lawsuit, on documents, in
about two months, for roughly the cost of one day of a lawyer's time.

This is rung five of the escalation ladder in `02-IP-ENFORCEMENT-PLAYBOOK`. Try
rung two first: a short message often recovers a domain from someone who registered
it as a supporter or by misunderstanding, and a UDRP complaint against that person
costs the Kingdom fifteen hundred dollars to obtain what an email would have got
free.

**This is an outline, not a pleading.** It sets out what must be proved, what
proves it, and what the process costs. The complaint itself is written to the
provider's supplemental rules and word limits, and for anything of value it is
worth having counsel or an experienced practitioner draft it. A losing complaint is
published permanently under the Kingdom's name.

## Before you send

- [ ] **The Kingdom has trademark rights, and can prove the date they arose.**
      A registration certificate is the clean case. Unregistered rights are
      accepted where the mark has become a distinctive identifier associated with
      the Kingdom's services, but they must be *proved* — evidence of use,
      duration, reach, advertising, media recognition, and public association. A
      bare assertion of common-law rights loses.
- [ ] **The domain was registered *after* the Kingdom's rights arose.** Check the
      registration date in WHOIS or RDAP against the Kingdom's first use and
      registration dates. Where the domain predates the Kingdom's rights, bad faith
      registration is close to impossible to establish and the complaint will fail.
      This is the single most common reason complaints are refused, and the check
      takes two minutes.
- [ ] **The domain is a gTLD or a ccTLD that has adopted the UDRP.** `.com`,
      `.org`, `.net`, `.info`, and all new gTLDs are covered. `.us` is not — it has
      its own usTLD policy with materially different elements. Most other ccTLDs run
      their own schemes. Confirm before drafting.
- [ ] **The registrar and registrant have been identified** from current WHOIS or
      RDAP output, captured and dated. Where a privacy or proxy service masks the
      registrant, file anyway; the registrar discloses the underlying registrant
      during verification and the complaint is amended.
- [ ] **The site and its history are captured in the Evidence Vault** — the current
      pages, the parking page or redirect, the MX records if email is configured,
      the historical captures from the Internet Archive, and the WHOIS history —
      each with its digest and custody record, per
      `05-EVIDENCE-AND-CHAIN-OF-CUSTODY` § 2. Capture before any contact. Sites
      change the moment a registrant learns they are being looked at, and a panel
      decides on the record as filed.
- [ ] **Any offer to sell has been preserved** in original form with full headers.
      An email offering the domain to the Kingdom for a sum above out-of-pocket
      costs is close to dispositive on bad faith, and it is the piece of evidence
      most often destroyed by a careless reply.
- [ ] **The respondent has no plausible legitimate interest** — they are not
      commonly known by the name, they are not making a bona fide offering under it,
      and this is not criticism or non-commercial commentary. Where the site is a
      genuine gripe site or a fan page with no commercial gain, take advice; panels
      split on these, and the Kingdom should not spend fifteen hundred dollars on a
      coin toss it will not enjoy losing publicly.
- [ ] **The Kingdom wants the domain, not money.** UDRP awards no damages, no fees,
      and no costs. If money is the point, this is the wrong forum.
- [ ] **The matter is open in the Enforcement Docket** with the Kingdom's own legal
      hold issued.

## The outline

```
UDRP COMPLAINT — WORKING OUTLINE
Matter: [MATTER REFERENCE]         Prepared: [DATE]          By: [OFFICER]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
0.  ADMINISTRATIVE PARTICULARS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Domain name(s) in dispute:   [DOMAIN]
    Registrar:                   [REGISTRAR NAME]
    Registration date:           [DATE FROM WHOIS/RDAP]
    Registrant of record:        [NAME / PRIVACY SERVICE]
    Provider selected:           [WIPO / FORUM / CAC / ADNDRC]
    Panel requested:             [SINGLE MEMBER / THREE MEMBER]
    Remedy sought:               [TRANSFER TO COMPLAINANT / CANCELLATION]
    Mutual jurisdiction elected: [LOCATION OF REGISTRAR'S PRINCIPAL
                                 OFFICE / REGISTRANT'S ADDRESS AS SHOWN
                                 IN WHOIS]
    Complainant:                 Apex Kingdom
    Authorized representative:   [NAME, OFFICE, ADDRESS, EMAIL, PHONE]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  THE COMPLAINANT AND ITS RIGHTS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    a.  What the Kingdom is, in three sentences. Plain, factual,
        verifiable. [DRAFT HERE]
    b.  The mark relied on:            [MARK]
        Registration number:           [NUMBER]        Annex [N]
        Register and date:             [PRINCIPAL, DATE]
        Classes and services:          [NUMBERS AND DESCRIPTION]
        First use in commerce:         [DATE]          Annex [N]
    c.  [IF UNREGISTERED: the evidence that the mark functions as a
        distinctive identifier — duration and scope of use, volume of
        services, advertising, media coverage, public recognition.
        Annexes [N]–[N].]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  ELEMENT ONE — IDENTICAL OR CONFUSINGLY SIMILAR   (Policy ¶ 4(a)(i))
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    To prove: the domain name is identical or confusingly similar to a
    trademark or service mark in which the Complainant has rights.

    a.  The Complainant has rights in [MARK]:  see § 1 above, Annex [N].
    b.  Side-by-side comparison, disregarding the TLD suffix:
            Mark:    [MARK]
            Domain:  [SECOND-LEVEL STRING]
        [STATE WHETHER IDENTICAL, OR WHAT WAS ADDED, OMITTED,
        TRANSPOSED, OR MISSPELLED — e.g., "the domain reproduces the mark
        in full with the descriptive term 'church' appended", or "the
        domain is a single-character misspelling of the mark".]
    c.  The mark remains recognizable within the domain name.

    Evidence:  registration certificate; WHOIS/RDAP extract showing the
               domain string; dated capture of the mark in use.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  ELEMENT TWO — NO RIGHTS OR LEGITIMATE INTERESTS  (Policy ¶ 4(a)(ii))
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    To prove: a prima facie case that the Respondent has no rights or
    legitimate interests in the domain name. The burden of production
    then shifts to the Respondent.

    a.  The Complainant has never licensed, authorized, or otherwise
        permitted the Respondent to use the mark or to register any
        domain incorporating it.
    b.  The Respondent is not commonly known by the domain name:
        [WHOIS registrant name differs; no corporate, trade name, or
        assumed name filing found; searches disclose no such use].
    c.  There is no bona fide offering of goods or services at the
        domain: [THE SITE IS PARKED / RESOLVES TO PAY-PER-CLICK LINKS /
        DOES NOT RESOLVE / REDIRECTS TO [DESTINATION] / IMITATES THE
        COMPLAINANT'S SITE].
    d.  The use is not legitimate noncommercial or fair use:
        [THE SITE CARRIES ADVERTISING / SOLICITS DONATIONS / OFFERS
        COMPETING SERVICES / IS NOT COMMENTARY OR CRITICISM].
    e.  [WHERE THE SITE IMPERSONATES: A domain used to impersonate the
        Complainant can confer no rights or legitimate interests.]

    Evidence:  dated captures of the resolving page; archive history;
               registrant-name searches; corporate and assumed-name
               register searches; the absence of any license.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  ELEMENT THREE — REGISTERED AND USED IN BAD FAITH (Policy ¶ 4(a)(iii))
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    To prove: BOTH bad faith registration AND bad faith use. Both.

    A.  Bad faith REGISTRATION
        i.   The Complainant's rights predate the registration:
             mark first used [DATE] / registered [DATE]; domain
             registered [DATE].                             Annex [N]
        ii.  The Respondent knew or must have known of the Complainant
             when registering: [THEY ARE LOCAL / THEY WERE A MEMBER OR
             FORMER OFFICER / THEY CORRESPONDED WITH THE KINGDOM ON
             [DATE] / THE MARK IS COINED AND HAS NO ORDINARY MEANING].

    B.  Bad faith USE — cite whichever of Policy ¶ 4(b) applies:
        ¶ 4(b)(i)   Registered primarily to sell, rent, or transfer to
                    the Complainant or a competitor for consideration
                    exceeding documented out-of-pocket costs.
                    [QUOTE THE OFFER, WITH DATE AND SUM.]    Annex [N]
        ¶ 4(b)(ii)  A pattern of registering domains to prevent mark
                    owners from reflecting their marks.
                    [LIST THE OTHER DOMAINS AND PRIOR DECISIONS.]
        ¶ 4(b)(iii) Registered primarily to disrupt the business of a
                    competitor.
        ¶ 4(b)(iv)  Intentional attempt to attract, for commercial gain,
                    internet users to the site by creating a likelihood
                    of confusion with the Complainant's mark as to
                    source, sponsorship, affiliation, or endorsement.
                    [DESCRIBE THE SITE AND WHAT IT OFFERS.] Annex [N]
        Other       [PASSIVE HOLDING WHERE THE MARK IS DISTINCTIVE, NO
                    PLAUSIBLE GOOD-FAITH USE EXISTS, AND THE RESPONDENT
                    HAS CONCEALED THEIR IDENTITY OR GIVEN FALSE CONTACT
                    DETAILS / MX RECORDS CONFIGURED, CREATING A RISK OF
                    EMAIL IMPERSONATION / FALSE WHOIS DATA / FAILURE TO
                    RESPOND TO THE COMPLAINANT'S CORRESPONDENCE.]

    Evidence:  WHOIS/RDAP with registration date; the offer to sell in
               original form with headers; dated captures; archive
               history; reverse-WHOIS showing other registrations; DNS
               and MX records; prior UDRP decisions against the same
               registrant.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5.  REMEDY AND CERTIFICATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    a.  Remedy requested: transfer of [DOMAIN] to the Complainant.
    b.  Mutual jurisdiction: the Complainant submits, with respect to
        any challenge to a decision to transfer or cancel, to the
        jurisdiction of the courts at [ELECTED LOCATION].
    c.  Certification that the information is complete and accurate,
        that the complaint is not being presented for any improper
        purpose, and that the assertions are warranted.
    d.  Signature of the Complainant or its authorized representative.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6.  ANNEX SCHEDULE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Annex 1  Certificate of registration, Reg. No. [NUMBER]
    Annex 2  WHOIS/RDAP extract for [DOMAIN], captured [DATE]
    Annex 3  Dated capture of the resolving page, [DATE]
    Annex 4  Internet Archive history for [DOMAIN]
    Annex 5  Correspondence with the Respondent
    Annex 6  Evidence of the Complainant's use of the mark since [DATE]
    Annex 7  [FURTHER]
    [Each annex cross-referenced to its Evidence Vault digest in the
    matter record — the digests are for the Kingdom's own file and do
    not appear in the filed complaint.]
```

## Notes

### The three elements, and which one actually decides the case

All three must be proved and the complainant carries the burden on each. In
practice element one is nearly always satisfied and element two is usually
satisfied by a competent prima facie showing. **Element three decides the matter**,
and it is conjunctive: the domain must have been *registered* in bad faith **and**
be *being used* in bad faith. A domain registered innocently and later put to a bad
use ordinarily fails, and — the point worth committing to memory — **a domain
registered before the Kingdom's trademark rights arose almost always fails**,
because the registrant cannot have targeted rights that did not yet exist. Check
the dates before spending a dollar.

Element two shifts. The complainant need only make out a prima facie case that the
respondent lacks rights or legitimate interests; the burden of production then
moves to the respondent, because the facts are within their knowledge. But the
respondent's safe harbours in Policy ¶ 4(c) are real: a bona fide offering made
before notice of the dispute, being commonly known by the name, or legitimate
non-commercial or fair use without intent for commercial gain to misleadingly
divert consumers or to tarnish the mark. If any of those plausibly applies, the
matter is not a UDRP case.

Panels decide on the documents alone. There is no hearing, no discovery, no
cross-examination, and no opportunity to fix a thin record. Everything the Kingdom
will ever get to say is in the complaint as filed.

### Choice of provider

The WIPO Arbitration and Mediation Center is the most established, has the deepest
published body of decisions, and maintains the *WIPO Jurisprudential Overview*,
which is the working reference for how panels actually decide these questions and
which should be consulted before drafting. Forum (formerly the National Arbitration
Forum) is US-based, marginally cheaper, and entirely respectable. The Czech
Arbitration Court and ADNDRC also handle gTLD disputes. For a Connecticut
complainant against a US registrant either WIPO or Forum is a sound choice; where
the respondent is outside the United States, WIPO's international standing is
worth the difference.

Single-member or three-member panel is the complainant's election. Single is the
default and is right for nearly everything at this scale. A three-member panel
roughly triples the fee and is worth it only where the matter is genuinely close,
the domain is valuable, or the respondent has already indicated they will fight.
Note that the respondent may elect three members even where the complainant asked
for one, in which case the fee is shared.

### What the remedy is, and what it is not

The panel may order **transfer** of the domain to the complainant, or
**cancellation**. That is the entire range of relief. Ask for transfer;
cancellation merely releases the name back into the pool for someone else to take.

There are no damages, no costs, no attorney's fees, no injunction against anything
other than the registration, and no finding the Kingdom can enforce elsewhere. The
proceeding decides who holds the domain and nothing more.

Where money genuinely matters, the alternative is the Anticybersquatting Consumer
Protection Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(d), in federal court, which permits statutory
damages of $1,000 to $100,000 per domain name under § 1117(d) and, where the
registrant cannot be found or served, an *in rem* action against the domain itself
under § 1125(d)(2). It costs many times what a UDRP costs and takes many times as
long. The UDRP is not a lesser version of it; it is a different instrument for a
different purpose, and for this organisation it is almost always the right one.

### Cost and timeline, realistically

**Cost.** Roughly USD 1,300–1,500 for a single-member panel covering one to five
domain names, and roughly USD 4,000–4,500 for a three-member panel. The complainant
pays the whole fee up front and does not recover it, whatever the outcome. Fee
schedules change; confirm the current one on the provider's site before budgeting.
Add drafting costs if counsel is engaged — a straightforward complaint is
commonly a flat fee in the low thousands and should be quoted as one.

**Timeline.** About two months from filing to a decision that has taken effect:

| Stage | Typical duration |
|---|---|
| Provider's formal compliance review | 2–5 days |
| Registrar verification and lock of the domain | Within days of filing |
| Commencement and notification of the respondent | On completion of the above |
| Respondent's period to reply | 20 days |
| Appointment of the panel | About 5 days after the reply period |
| Decision | Within 14 days of appointment |
| Implementation by the registrar | 10 business days after the decision |

The domain is locked by the registrar on filing, so it cannot be transferred away
mid-proceeding. Most respondents at this scale do not reply at all; default does
not win the case automatically — the panel still tests the three elements — but it
removes the only source of contrary evidence.

Under Policy ¶ 4(k) the respondent may, within ten business days of a decision to
transfer, commence a court action in the elected mutual jurisdiction, and the
registrar will then hold the domain pending the outcome. This is rare. It is the
reason the mutual jurisdiction election in § 0 of the outline matters, and the
reason it should ordinarily be the location of the registrar's principal office
rather than a distant foreign address.

### Two cautions

**Decisions are published, permanently, and indexed.** Every UDRP decision appears
on the provider's site under the parties' names and is found by anyone who searches
for the Kingdom afterwards. A well-founded complaint that succeeds is a public
record of the Kingdom enforcing its rights competently — genuinely useful. A
speculative one that fails is a permanent, searchable document explaining why the
Kingdom's claim to its own name was rejected.

**Reverse Domain Name Hijacking.** Where a panel concludes that a complaint was
brought in bad faith — typically to harass the registrant, or in the face of an
obvious defect such as a domain registered years before the complainant's rights
arose — Rule 15(e) requires the panel to declare it in the published decision.
There is no fine, and the reputational damage is entirely sufficient. It is avoided
by the same discipline that wins the case: check the dates, capture the evidence,
and do not file against someone with a plausible legitimate interest.

### What this is not

A UDRP complaint is a filing in a contractual arbitration to which the respondent
agreed when they registered the domain. The Kingdom appears in it as a complainant
asserting trademark rights, not as a sovereign, a government, or a tribunal, and
the complaint should carry no seal, title, or assertion of authority beyond
ownership of the mark. Nothing in this process gives the Kingdom power to summon,
order, or penalise anyone; what it gives is a decision by a neutral panel that a
registrar will implement. That is enough, and it is a great deal more than the
alternative.
